edge_898.relationship: Reciprocal comparison of Eurasian cores, joined to connections in a polycentric world (2000)
edge_898.evidence_note: Pomeranz's own statement of method, The Great Divergence (2000), introduction (pp. 3–27 read; later-edition pagination). Comparisons between scattered core regions should be 'truly reciprocal' (p. 8), 'viewing both sides of the comparison as “deviations” when seen through the expectations of the other, rather than leaving one as always the norm' (p. 8). With Tilly's 'encompassing comparison', 'comparison and the analysis of connections become indistinguishable' (p. 10). 'Thus the book combines comparative analysis, some purely local contingency, and an integrative or global approach', and before 1800 'we have, instead, a polycentric world with no dominant center' (p. 4). The introduction ends 'with connections and interactions explaining what comparison alone cannot' (p. 25). He places the book as 'joining the burgeoning field of “world history,”' while warning that it 'treats the world’s regions very unevenly' and that 'adding a few Chinese and Japanese foils to a European story does not make it “world history”' (p. 25). A contribution, not a founding: the approach was 'anticipated in important ways by my colleague R. Bin Wong' (p. 7), and 'Here, too, I am following a procedure outlined in Wong’s recent China Transformed' (p. 8); the encompassing comparison is Tilly's (p. 10, n. 14). Huang's 2002 critique and Pomeranz's reply are later readings, not evidence for this edge.

edge_899.relationship: Coal and New World resources enabled divergence between comparably developed Eurasian cores (2000)
edge_899.evidence_note: Pomeranz's own argument, The Great Divergence (2000), introduction (pp. 3–27 read; later-edition pagination). He takes 'Why wasn’t England the Yangzi Delta?' as seriously as 'Why wasn’t the Yangzi Delta England?' and argues 'that Europe, too, could have wound up on an “east Asian,” labor-intensive path', a result avoided through 'sharp discontinuities, based on both fossil fuels and access to New World resources' (p. 13). 'Constraints connected to energy, and ultimately to quantities of land (particularly the shrinking forests of core areas throughout Eurasia), were a far more important looming impediment to further growth' than capital (p. 19). The Atlantic trade mattered for 'how much they relieved the strain on Europe’s supply of what was truly scarce: land and energy', and 'the fruits of overseas exploitation were probably roughly as important to at least Britain’s economic transformation as its epochal turn to fossil fuels' (p. 23). The book uses 'the fruits of overseas coercion' to explain the difference from China and Japan, 'not the whole of that development' (p. 4). Cooper's 2000 review (read in full) summarises it in the same year: 'Europe had more institutional slack, easier access to coal (which was crucial, in the author's view), and cheap imports of sugar and cotton harvested by slaves in its New World colonies', and objects that Pomeranz 'relies heavily on plausible guesstimates'. The earlier Making of a Hinterland (1993) already argued, in the publisher's description, 'that the development of certain regions entailed the systematic underdevelopment of other regions'; Bianco (1996, p. 243, read) notes that it 'ne sépare jamais l'enquête régionale du débat théorique', including Huang's involution model. A contribution, not a founding: earlier arguments from colonial extraction (Williams 1944, Frank 1969, Amin 1974) are cited at p. 3, n. 2, and he notes parallels with Sugihara (p. 12). Huang's 2002 critique and Pomeranz's reply are later readings, not evidence for this edge.

nationaltradition.label: National & imperial narratives
nationaltradition.description: National and imperial histories join source work to competing accounts of peoples, states, liberty and civilization. Michelet, Macaulay and Bancroft differ in method and purpose; colonial hierarchies, liberation histories and critiques of nationalist exclusions remain in tension.
nationaltradition.representative_figures_and_works: A broad context of historical production, not one school: nation-building, colonial institutions, and resistance generate different and often conflicting projects.

economic.label: Economic history
economic.date_label: 1800s roots · Economic History Society founded 1926 · multiple paradigms
economic.description: Competing explanations investigate institutions, prices and incomes, class relations, growth, households, slavery and empire. Serial history and cliometrics use different questions and models. North’s incentives differ from Polanyi’s historically specific market society; Gerschenkron questions repeated industrial paths; de Vries connects household labor and demand; Pomeranz combines regional comparison with global resource relations.
economic.representative_figures_and_works: Nineteenth-century roots include classical political economy and the German historical school (e.g. Schmoller); twentieth-century examples include R. H. Tawney, Eileen Power, and Douglass North. Further approaches include Polanyi, The Great Transformation (1944); Gerschenkron, Economic Backwardness in Historical Perspective (1962 collection); de Vries’s industrious-revolution article (1994); Pomeranz, The Great Divergence (2000). E. A. Wrigley: People, Cities and Wealth (1987); Continuity, Chance and Change (1988).

strands.title: Regional comparison and global divergence
strands.focus: Pomeranz compares developed regions within Eurasia and connects divergence with coal and overseas resources, avoiding an undifferentiated Europe-versus-Asia contrast.

strands.title: Material life, markets and capitalism
strands.focus: Braudel distinguishes overlapping economic activities and geographically centered world-economies. His disagreement with Weber and selective Wallerstein dialogue are attributed arguments, not a settled universal history.

strands.title: Agrarian change and documentary comparability

strands.title: Women’s work, household forms and economic change

strands.title: Domestic service as an economic question

strands.title: Brazilian income flows and structural criticism

strands.title: Managerial coordination and the scale of activity
strands.focus: Chandler’s selected opening links new energy, transport and communication capacities to the conditions for administrative coordination. Earlier growth and specialization could remain compatible with owner-managed firms and market exchange.

strands.title: Artisans and uneven industrialization in India
strands.focus: Roy examines five crafts rather than treating textile decline as universal. His introduction distinguishes family work, wage labour, markets and organizational change, while acknowledging that adaptation did not yield development comparable to Europe or Japan.

strands.title: Firms, inventions and forms of work
strands.focus: Compare Chandler’s American enterprise scale, Mokyr’s British technological change and Roy’s Indian artisanal reorganization. These explanations concern different units and periods; none supplies a universal sequence from household to large factory.
strands.works: Chandler (1977); Mokyr (1999); Roy (1999), selected primary passages

strands.title: Railroads and the meaning of social saving
strands.focus: McClelland contests identifying measured transport savings with the railroad’s entire contribution to growth. His notes question the relation between observed freight prices and marginal costs under altered traffic and competition.

strands.title: Slavery productivity and a contested inference
strands.focus: Fogel and Engerman’s opening specifies a total-factor-productivity index. David and Temin argue that national-price aggregation across differing crop mixes need not rank technical efficiency: climate, prices and risk complicate the inference.

strands.title: Household production and disputed divergence
strands.focus: Pomeranz challenges Huang’s involution thesis and compares household labor with industrious change. Huang’s later review argues that output growth can conceal diminishing returns to work; Pomeranz’s reply opening rejects one necessary path to development.

strands.title: Coal, constraints and competing explanations
strands.focus: Pomeranz links accessible energy and colonial resources to relief of land constraints. Huang questions whether coal availability explains divergence or industrial demand explains coal development. The exchange leaves causal weights open to examination.

strands.title: Wealth and the measurement of goods
strands.focus: Weatherill acknowledges Shammas’s challenge: ownership patterns associated with occupation or towns may reflect wealth. Their different data constructions ask different questions.

economic.scope_note: Distinguish the relevant historians, evidence, and mechanisms before claiming an influence. A subject shared with Annales or Marxism is not itself an explanation. Institutional approaches are not interchangeable, and consumption does not replace production. Household interests can conflict. Gerschenkron’s European comparison and Pomeranz’s Eurasian argument have distinct scales; neither is a universal development law. Furtado’s demand analysis and Novais’s structural criticism offer a Brazilian exchange, with primary-edition and numerical verification limits retained.

political.label: Political history
political.description: Examines institutions, diplomacy and struggles over power through different methods. Namier reconstructs parliamentary connections; Benson studies voters; Tilly investigates collective claims; Hunt joins political symbols and social identities. Hill, Dorothy Thompson and Flexner examine radical and rights politics, while Guha and Cooper investigate insurgency and labor under colonial rule. These approaches overlap without replacing all earlier political history.

women.label: Women’s history
women.date_label: Nineteenth-century and interwar work; renewed expansion from the 1960s
women.description: Studies women as historical actors and examines work, family, politics, and structures of power. Earlier scholarship, activism, teaching, and documentary collecting precede the field’s expansion alongside later feminist movements. Recovery, institutional growth, rediscovery, and methodological disagreement overlap; this is not a field created from nothing in the 1960s or one account of a shared female experience.

Growth stages, democratic legitimacy and political institutionalization answer different questions. Eisenstadt’s later multiple-modernities program disputes convergence on one Western pattern while retaining comparative inquiry.

modern.scope_note: Economic stages, communication and social dispositions, institutional differentiation, and democratization are distinct explanations. These contributors are not all historians, and the models do not form one inevitable path. Lipset explicitly denies automatic democratization, Huntington prioritizes institutional capacity, and Eisenstadt’s 2000 argument revises convergence assumptions. These differences do not erase hierarchical categories, Cold War purposes or disputed empirical claims in earlier models; a later program is not projected into every 1950s text.

social.label: New social history
social.description: An overlapping field of work, class formation, households, community and collective action. Thompson, Davis and Gutman already integrate culture and agency; demographic and mobility studies use distinct evidence. Davidoff and Hall connect gender and middle-class life; Chakrabarty and Cooper investigate colonial labor and the limits of inherited categories. Scott’s critique makes experience itself a historical question, not something to discard.

Thompson and Eric Hobsbawm; Herbert Gutman, Work, Culture, and Society in Industrializing America (1976); Natalie Zemon Davis, Society and Culture in Early Modern France (1975); Charles Tilly; E. A. Wrigley and historical demography. Earlier social inquiry provides comparisons, not membership in a later school. Further readings: Davidoff and Hall, Family Fortunes (1987); Chakrabarty, Rethinking Working-Class History (1989); Scott, “The Evidence of Experience” (1991); Cooper, Decolonization and African Society (1996). Geoff Eley and Keith Nield: “Why does social history ignore politics?” (1980).

gender.description: Examines gender as a historically changing organization of social relations, identities and power. sts.label: Science and technology studies / STS
sts.description: An interdisciplinary field examining how knowledge, technologies, institutions, and social arrangements develop together. Historical, sociological, ethnographic, and policy-oriented inquiries coexist. SSK and laboratory studies contribute to STS but do not define its entire scope. Knorr Cetina’s comparative laboratory cultures, Harding’s feminist epistemology, and Sussex/Cornell institution building add distinct approaches and histories.

Petersen, and Trevor Pinch, eds., Handbook of Science and Technology Studies (1995); Bruno Latour and Steve Woolgar, Laboratory Life (1979). kenneth_pomeranz.label: Kenneth Pomeranz
kenneth_pomeranz.date_label: The Making of a Hinterland 1993 · The Great Divergence 2000
kenneth_pomeranz.description: A historian of China whose reciprocal comparisons of Eurasian core regions recast the divergence of European and Chinese economies. The Great Divergence (2000) takes 'Why wasn’t England the Yangzi Delta?' as seriously as the reverse question and argues that 'Europe, too, could have wound up on an “east Asian,” labor-intensive path'. Coal, and land-intensive goods from New World colonies worked by enslaved people, relieved Europe's constraints of land and energy. The earlier Making of a Hinterland (1993) traces the economic and ecological costs for inland North China when the late Qing and Republican state abandoned many hinterland areas.
kenneth_pomeranz.representative_figures_and_works: Kenneth Pomeranz (b. 1958); The Making of a Hinterland: State, Society, and Economy in Inland North China, 1853–1937 (1993); The Great Divergence: China, Europe, and the Making of the Modern World Economy (2000). Readings: Bianco's review (1996); Cooper's review (2000); Huang's critique and Pomeranz's reply (2002).
kenneth_pomeranz.scope_note: This entry presents the argument of The Great Divergence as its introduction states it (pp. 3–27 read, with the contents, in a preview of the later Princeton edition; page numbers are that edition's). The Making of a Hinterland is checked at contents level and through Bianco's 1996 review, read in full; its text is unread. He is not presented as the originator of reciprocal comparison: he writes that the approach was 'anticipated in important ways by my colleague R. Bin Wong', takes the 'encompassing comparison' from Charles Tilly, and notes parallels with Sugihara Kaoru. Arguments from colonial extraction (Williams, Frank, Amin) precede his. His estimates are contested: Cooper (2000) notes 'plausible guesstimates', and Bianco (1996) judges that the 1993 book 'postule plus qu'il ne prouve' a deliberate strategy of selective development. Huang's 2002 critique and Pomeranz's reply are later readings, not evidence for the 2000 argument.
